title: Charlie Kirk Was Shot a Year Ago. The Conspiracy Theories Are More Rampant Than Ever
gist: A year after Charlie Kirk's assassination, conspiracy content built around it has become a self-sustaining business, with Candace Owens accumulating hundreds of millions of views and researchers measuring a statistically significant surge in death threats traceable to her output. Platform incentives on X and YouTube keep the niche monetizable, and experts expect escalation through the upcoming Tyler Robinson trial, while Turning Point argues the influence is already collapsing.

themes.theme: Conspiracy content as a business model

insights.claim: Conspiracy content about a single assassination has accumulated hundreds of millions of views for one influencer over a monthslong campaign, demonstrating that a single tragedy can anchor a durable creator revenue stream.
insights.speaker: David Gilbert
insights.so_what: View volumes at this scale represent real ad and subscription revenue, meaning platform enforcement decisions have direct P&L consequences for a class of creators.
insights.locator: But ultimately, the baseless claim that persisted

insights.claim: X and YouTube remain environments where speculation about the killing can both recruit new audiences and be monetized, which is the structural reason the content keeps being produced.
insights.speaker: David Gilbert
insights.so_what: Audience acquisition plus monetization in the same surface is the mechanism; platforms that break either half change creator economics for this category overnight.
insights.quote: X and YouTube are rife with speculation about Kirk’s death, where it is both still possible to recruit new audiences and monetize them

insights.claim: The personalities driving these theories were largely unknown and financially broke before the assassination, and the content is explicitly described by a Turning Point spokesperson as their moneymaker, explaining why they will not stop regardless of pressure.
insights.speaker: David Gilbert
insights.so_what: Financial dependence means moral appeals fail and only demonetization or deplatforming changes behavior — relevant to how platform trust-and-safety spend actually works.
insights.quote: They won’t stop because many of these personalities were completely unknown and broke before Charlie was killed, and this is their moneymaker

insights.claim: The appeal of conspiratorial explanations is that they make events seem more mysterious and exciting, and for many audiences that framing is simply preferable to the reality of violence committed by a solo individual.
insights.speaker: David Gilbert
insights.so_what: Demand-side preference, not supply-side deception, is the driver — which means suppression of supply reliably fails to reduce belief.
insights.quote: For many, her explanations are preferable to the reality of an act of violence by a solo individual.
insights.locator: The result is that Kirk’s death has become yet another rabbit hole

insights.claim: Researchers at the Network Contagion Research Institute found that one influencer caused a measurable, statistically significant surge in death threats and calls for violence against the victim's widow.
insights.speaker: David Gilbert
insights.so_what: Quantified attribution of offline threats to a named account is the evidentiary foundation platforms and courts need to act, raising legal and advertiser risk for hosting services.
insights.quote: Candace Owens caused a measurable, statistically significant surge in death threats and calls for violence against [Charlie Kirk’s wife] Erika Kirk.
insights.locator: There have already been real-world repercussions

insights.claim: A man was arrested in May for allegedly threatening to kill the victim's widow ahead of her appearance at a Turning Point USA event in San Antonio, though he had not yet been charged.
insights.speaker: David Gilbert
insights.so_what: Event security and insurance costs for politically exposed organizations rise directly with this kind of incident frequency.
insights.locator: In May, a man was arrested

insights.claim: The organization the victim cofounded has repeatedly and publicly called on the influencers spreading the rumors to stop, and those calls have not been heeded.
insights.speaker: David Gilbert
insights.so_what: Even in-group authority cannot discipline the conspiracy economy once it has independent distribution and revenue, a limit on self-regulation as a governance model.

insights.claim: A senior researcher at Open Measures expects the conspiracy theories to escalate further rather than fade, because the criminal trial of the accused killer will run over the next year, draw major media attention, and supply conspiracy theorists with fresh material.
insights.speaker: David Gilbert
insights.so_what: A scheduled trial is a forecastable engagement catalyst — platforms, advertisers and security teams can plan around a known window of elevated activity.
insights.quote: There’s no reason to believe conspiracy theories about Kirk’s murder will lose steam anytime soon
insights.locator: Experts believe these conspiracy theories will continue

insights.claim: A Turning Point spokesperson argues the opposite trajectory, saying the theories already have much less reach and potency than six months ago and that the influence and credibility of those promoting them have collapsed and will keep collapsing.
insights.speaker: David Gilbert
insights.so_what: The gap between the researcher and insider forecasts is itself the tradeable question: whether conspiracy audiences compound or decay after the initial shock.
insights.quote: The conspiracy theories have much less reach and potency now than they did six months ago, and I think I’ll say the same six months from now
insights.locator: “The conspiracy theories have much less reach and potency now

insights.claim: Conspiratorial belief around assassinations is historically normal in the US, with nearly 80 percent of Americans in the 1970s believing a conspiracy rather than a lone gunman was behind the JFK killing and majorities holding that view for decades.
insights.speaker: David Gilbert
insights.so_what: A ~80 percent historical base rate suggests current levels are not anomalous, which argues against attributing the phenomenon primarily to social media platforms.
insights.quote: Majorities of Americans have believed for decades that JFK was killed by a conspiracy rather than by a lone gunman.

insights.claim: Many competing theories emerged immediately after the killing — a false flag to deflect from Epstein-related attention, a fully staged event, an AI-powered gun, the shooter being a supporter, and the victim still being alive — but only one narrative ultimately survived at scale.
insights.speaker: David Gilbert
insights.so_what: Conspiracy narratives compete and consolidate like products; the winner is determined by promoter distribution, not internal plausibility.

insights.claim: The surviving narrative holds that someone close to the victim or acting on behalf of Israel was responsible, that the accused is a patsy, and that the actual weapon was an exploding microphone.
insights.speaker: David Gilbert
insights.so_what: The winning version incorporates an existing antisemitic template, showing that narratives which plug into pre-existing prejudice distribute more efficiently.

insights.claim: In the minutes after the shooting, graphic video was ubiquitous, far-right figures called for violence and vengeance, and right-wing lawmakers and influencers demanded the cancellation of anyone celebrating, with conspiracy theories arriving only afterward.
insights.speaker: David Gilbert
insights.so_what: The observed sequence — graphic content, then retaliation calls, then conspiracy formation — is a repeatable template platforms can pre-plan moderation around for future violent events.
